body:
Electricity as an energy carrier

Electricity is a convenient form of energy used for lighting, heating, cooling, communication, transport and industrial production. It can be generated from several primary energy sources and delivered through an interconnected network to consumers.

Coal, natural gas, flowing water, sunlight, wind and uranium are examples of energy resources. Electricity produced from them is generally described as a secondary form of energy because another energy source is converted into electrical energy.

An electricity system has 4 essential functions: generation, transmission, distribution and system operation. Generation produces electrical energy. Transmission transfers large quantities of power over considerable distances. Distribution delivers electricity to consumers. System operation coordinates supply, demand and network conditions so that the entire system remains stable.

Power and energy are different quantities

Power measures the rate at which energy is generated or consumed. Its unit is the watt (W), commonly expressed as kilowatts (kW) or megawatts (MW). Energy measures the total quantity generated or consumed over time. Electricity consumption is commonly measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh).

For equipment operating at constant power:

Energy in kWh = Power in kW × Operating time in hours.

Understanding an electricity bill

A 1 kW appliance operating for 3 hours consumes 3 kWh. In electricity billing, 1 unit ordinarily means 1 kWh. Therefore, the appliance consumes 3 units, not 3 kW.

Installed capacity describes the rated power-generating capability of a plant. Generation describes the electricity actually produced during a specified period. A 100 MW plant need not generate 100 MWh every hour: maintenance, fuel availability, water availability, sunlight, wind and demand can affect actual output.

Why electricity must be coordinated continuously

Consumers switch appliances and machines on and off throughout the day. Consequently, demand changes continuously. In the interconnected grid, electricity generation and consumption must remain closely balanced, while sufficient transmission capacity must be available to carry power to the required locations.

Electricity can be stored indirectly in batteries or pumped-storage facilities, but ordinary power lines do not provide large-scale storage. A generating station therefore cannot simply produce unlimited electricity regardless of demand and network conditions.

Rooftop solar systems and other distributed generators can also produce electricity near consumers. Subject to applicable interconnection and metering arrangements, a consumer may use this electricity locally and sometimes export surplus energy to the distribution network.

Prelims focus

  • Generation produces electricity; transmission transfers bulk power; distribution supplies consumers.
  • Power is measured in W, kW or MW; electrical energy is measured in Wh, kWh or MWh.
  • 1 electricity billing unit ordinarily equals 1 kWh.
  • Installed generating capacity and actual electricity generation are not interchangeable.
  • Trap: A 100 MW power station does not necessarily produce 100 MW of power at every moment.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 6, Electricity and Circuits, printed pp. 116–119; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Work and Energy, Chapter 11; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Infrastructure, Chapter 8, section on energy.]

title: Understanding the Electricity System: From Energy Source to Consumer

body:
How electricity is generated

Electricity generation converts energy from another source into electrical energy. In many power stations, a turbine rotates a generator. The generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy through electromagnetic induction. Solar photovoltaic cells are an important exception: they convert sunlight directly into electrical energy without a rotating turbine.

Major electricity-generation technologies

SourceBasic conversionImportant operating condition
Coal or natural gasFuel energy produces heat or drives a turbine, which operates a generator.Requires fuel and suitable plant availability.
HydropowerMoving or falling water rotates a turbine and generator.Depends on water availability and operating restrictions.
Nuclear powerHeat released by nuclear fission is used to generate electricity through a power-conversion system.Requires a functioning nuclear generating station and fuel.
Wind powerWind turns a rotor connected to a generator.Output varies with wind conditions.
Solar photovoltaic powerSolar cells convert sunlight into direct-current electricity.Output depends on sunlight and weather.

Solar photovoltaic (PV) systems generally use an inverter to convert direct current (DC) into alternating current (AC) suitable for an AC network. Solar thermal electricity generation differs from solar PV because it uses solar heat in a power-conversion process.

Dispatchable and variable generation

Dispatchable generation can adjust its output when instructed, within the physical limits of the plant and the availability of fuel or water. A reservoir-based hydroelectric station can often increase or decrease generation relatively quickly, provided sufficient water and operating permission are available.

Variable renewable generation, particularly wind and solar PV, depends on changing natural conditions. Its maximum available output cannot be increased on demand merely by an instruction from the grid operator. However, such plants may reduce output when instructed, and storage can help shift their energy to another time.

Thermal and nuclear stations can provide substantial electricity, but their ability to change output quickly differs by technology and operating condition. A run-of-river hydroelectric project is also more dependent on immediate river flow than a reservoir-based project.

Electricity storage and the generation mix

A battery stores previously supplied electrical energy in chemical form and releases it later. Pumped-storage hydropower uses electricity to pump water to a higher reservoir and later recovers part of that energy by allowing water to flow through a turbine. Neither technology creates energy without an input; both have conversion losses.

A diverse generation mix can improve reliability because different sources have different strengths and limitations. Solar power is available during daylight, wind generation depends on wind conditions, and suitably equipped conventional or storage resources can help meet demand when variable generation is low.

Renewable, low-carbon and dispatchable describe different characteristics. Nuclear power is low-carbon during operation but is not conventionally classified as renewable. Solar PV is renewable but naturally variable. Reservoir hydropower is renewable and can often be dispatchable.

Prelims focus

  • A rotating electrical generator works through electromagnetic induction.
  • Solar PV converts sunlight directly into electricity; it does not require a steam turbine.
  • An inverter converts DC into AC.
  • Reservoir hydropower and run-of-river hydropower have different operating flexibility.
  • Battery and pumped-storage systems store energy; they are not primary energy resources.
  • Trap: Renewable generation is not always fully controllable, and low-carbon generation is not necessarily renewable.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 10, Sources of Energy, Chapter 14, and Magnetic Effects of Electric Current, Chapter 13; NCERT, Contemporary India II, Class 10, Minerals and Energy Resources, section on energy resources; International Energy Agency, Energy Transitions Require Innovation in Power System Planning, section on system adequacy, consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Electricity Generation: Sources, Conversion and Availability

body:
Why electricity is transmitted at high voltage

Power stations are often located far from the cities, villages and industries they serve. A transmission network carries large quantities of power across these distances.

For a given amount of transmitted power, using a higher voltage generally allows a lower current. This is important because current flowing through a conductor produces heat. The power lost as resistive heating is proportional to the square of the current, expressed as I2R, where I is current and R is resistance.

If current is reduced to half while resistance remains unchanged, resistive heating loss becomes one-fourth. This illustrates the advantage of high-voltage transmission. Actual power-system losses also depend on other factors, so transmission losses cannot be calculated from this observation alone.

How transformers help deliver power

Most conventional electricity networks use alternating current (AC). A transformer can increase or decrease AC voltage through electromagnetic induction. Near a generating station, a step-up transformer raises voltage for bulk transmission. Substations closer to consumers reduce voltage in stages.

A transformer does not change the grid's frequency. In particular, stepping voltage down does not convert 50 Hz electricity into another frequency. A conventional transformer also cannot directly transform steady DC in the same manner as AC.

Transmission and distribution perform different functions

FeatureTransmissionDistribution
Main functionTransfers bulk electrical power between generating stations and major substations or networks.Delivers power from distribution networks to end users.
Typical componentsHigh-voltage lines, towers, grid substations and interconnections.Distribution feeders, local transformers, service lines and consumer meters.
Usual scaleLong-distance and large power transfers.Local or regional electricity delivery.
Operational concernBulk transfer capability, system stability and major network faults.Local outages, voltage quality, consumer connections and billing.

The boundary between transmission and distribution is determined by the applicable network and regulatory arrangements, not by one universal voltage value. A feeder is a circuit that supplies a defined part of a network. A distribution transformer reduces voltage for local consumer supply.

AC and high-voltage DC transmission

High-voltage direct current (HVDC) is also used for certain long-distance bulk transfers and for connecting systems where controlled power transfer is useful. It requires conversion equipment between AC and DC. Therefore, the statement that all long-distance electricity transmission uses AC is incorrect.

Why substations matter

A substation may change voltage, switch circuits, measure power flow and provide protection. Circuit breakers interrupt fault currents when instructed by protective equipment. These functions allow a complex network to supply different locations and isolate many faults without switching off every connected consumer.

Prelims focus

  • High-voltage transmission generally reduces current for a given transferred power and therefore reduces resistive heating loss.
  • Resistive power loss is proportional to the square of current when resistance is unchanged.
  • A step-up transformer increases AC voltage; a step-down transformer decreases it.
  • Transformers do not change the supply frequency.
  • HVDC is an important exception to predominantly AC transmission networks.
  • Trap: A distribution transformer reduces voltage; it does not generate electricity.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 10, Electricity, Chapter 11, printed pp. 172–173 and subsequent sections on resistance and electrical power; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Magnetic Effects of Electric Current, Chapter 13; Central Electricity Authority, Functions, technical standards and power-system responsibilities, consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The relationship between current and resistive heating loss.

title: Transmission, Substations and Distribution of Electricity

body:
Demand changes continuously

Electricity demand is the combined power requirement of consumers at a particular moment. It changes with the time of day, season, temperature, agricultural pumping, industrial activity and consumer behaviour.

Peak demand is the highest demand recorded during a defined period. The amount of energy consumed over a day is different from the maximum power needed at any one moment. A system may have sufficient daily energy but still face difficulty supplying a short period of exceptionally high demand.

What electricity dispatch means

Dispatch is the coordination of electricity generation and other available resources to meet demand while respecting network security and operational constraints. Power-system operators forecast demand, schedule generation, monitor actual conditions and direct necessary adjustments.

The system does not necessarily use every generating station at its maximum possible output. Some plants may be unavailable, some may be more costly to operate, and some may be constrained by transmission capacity. The operator must consider system security in addition to energy cost.

Why frequency is important

India's interconnected AC grid has a nominal frequency of 50 Hz. Grid frequency reflects the balance between electrical power supplied and power consumed, including losses, across the interconnected system.

  • When demand exceeds available generation: frequency tends to fall, unless other controls compensate.
  • When generation exceeds demand: frequency tends to rise, unless other controls compensate.
  • When the imbalance is corrected: system controls work to return frequency close to its nominal value.

Under Regulation 30 of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission's Indian Electricity Grid Code, 2023, the national reference frequency is 50.000 Hz and the stated allowable band is 49.900–50.050 Hz. Operators are directed to endeavour to maintain frequency near 50 Hz and restore it within the allowable band when it moves outside. The same band was described in a CERC order issued in 2025. These are regulatory operating provisions, not a claim that frequency can never temporarily move outside the band.

How the grid is balanced

Operators use several responses when actual demand differs from forecasts:

  • Adjust output from available generating stations.
  • Call on operating reserves, including resources capable of responding quickly.
  • Use available storage or modify scheduled transfers where feasible.
  • Arrange demand reduction or demand shifting when suitable arrangements exist.
  • As a protective or emergency measure, shed some load when necessary to prevent a wider system failure.

Solar and wind generation make forecasting especially important because their available output changes with the weather. Storage and flexible demand can help move electricity use toward periods of greater renewable generation.

Who operates the interconnected grid?

At the national level, the National Load Despatch Centre (NLDC) coordinates the integrated national power system. Regional Load Despatch Centres (RLDCs) supervise and coordinate regional operations. State Load Despatch Centres (SLDCs) coordinate integrated power-system operations within their respective states. Grid Controller of India Limited, also known as GRID-INDIA, performs national and regional grid-operation functions.

Frequency concerns the timing of the AC cycle and overall power balance. Voltage concerns electrical potential difference. Low voltage at one location does not automatically mean the entire national grid has low frequency.

Prelims focus

  • India's nominal AC grid frequency is 50 Hz.
  • The Indian Electricity Grid Code, 2023, specifies a frequency band of 49.900–50.050 Hz in Regulation 30.
  • Demand greater than available generation tends to lower frequency; surplus generation tends to raise it.
  • NLDC operates at national level, RLDC at regional level and SLDC at state level.
  • Load shedding is a control or protective action, not electricity generation.
  • Trap: Peak demand is measured in power units such as MW, whereas daily electrical energy is measured in MWh or similar energy units.

[Sources: Central Electricity Regulatory Commission, Statement of Reasons for Indian Electricity Grid Code Regulations, 2023, Regulation 30, printed pp. 102–103; CERC, Order in Petition 9/SM/2025, discussion of grid frequency; GRID-INDIA, About Grid-India, functions of NLDC and RLDCs, consulted 16 November 2026.]
